sentences.text: Brachiosaurus was a quadrupedal dinosaur characterized by a small skull, long neck, large trunk, muscular tail, and slender columnar limbs.
The specific name altithorax means "deep chest", while the generic name Brachiosaurus means "arm lizard" due to its long forelimbs.
Researchers D'Emic and Carrano estimated the Brachiosaurus skull to be 70 centimeters long, 55 centimeters tall, and 35 centimeters wide.
The preserved humerus measures 204 cm in length, with an estimated original length of 216 cm after accounting for erosion.
The estimated length of Brachiosaurus is 26 meters.
Brachiosaurus likely ate ginkgos, conifers, tree ferns, and large cycads, consuming an estimated 200 to 400 kilograms of plant matter daily.
The genus Brachiosaurus was first described by Elmer S. Riggs in 1903.
Brachiosaurus fossils were first found in the Colorado River valley in western Colorado, United States.
The holotype specimen comes from the Brushy Basin Member of the Morrison Formation and dates to about 154 to 153 million years ago.
A Brachiosaurus skull was discovered in 1883 by farmer Marshall Parker Felch near Garden Park, Colorado.
Large-scale expeditions in German East Africa discovered significant brachiosaurid fossils in the Tendaguru Formation between 1909 and 1912.
While Brachiosaurus was once thought to be ectothermic due to its size, recent research suggests it was warm-blooded.
Brachiosaurus was adapted for a terrestrial lifestyle with slender limbs, a high chest, wide hips, high ilia, and a short tail.
In 1990, Stephen Czerkas hypothesized that Brachiosaurus occasionally entered water to thermoregulate.
In 1999, Olivier Rieppel and Christopher Brochu defended the near-vertical neck posture of Brachiosaurus, citing its long forelimbs and upward-sloping backbone.
In 2001, Gunga and Kirsch concluded that Brachiosaurus moved its neck laterally more often than vertically while feeding.
Brachiosaurus used a bird-like respiratory system with air sacs to achieve unidirectional airflow in its lungs.
In 2012, Carballido and colleagues reconstructed the growth of Brachiosaurus using a 2-meter-long juvenile skeleton named Toni.
The name Giraffatitan was elevated to full genus status by George Olshevsky in 1991 based on differences in vertebral variation.
A 1997 study by Leonardo Salgado suggested that Brachiosaurus and related genera were not a separate branch but offshoots of the Titanosauriformes stem group.
Brachiosaurus lived during the Late Jurassic period, from the Kimmeridgian to the Tithonian stages.
Brachiosaurus lived during the Kimmeridgian and Tithonian ages, between 155.6 and 145.5 million years ago.

There is a debate regarding neck length, with Gregory S. Paul suggesting it was shorter than Giraffatitan's in 1988, while Mike P. Taylor argued in 2009 that vertebrae proportions indicated otherwise.
There is an ongoing debate about whether the neck posture of Brachiosaurus was near-vertical or horizontal.
In 2016, Hallett and Wedel rejected the hypothesis that Brachiosaurus nostrils were at the snout tip, suggesting they were placed at the top of the head as traditionally thought.
In 2001, Lawrence M. Witmer argued that the fleshy nostrils of Brachiosaurus were likely placed at the front of the bony opening, similar to modern land animals.

Czerkas speculated that the large nasal opening of Brachiosaurus may have housed tissue for enhanced smelling, noting that the exact location of the nostrils remains inconclusive without skin impressions.
